```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(yardstick)
metrics_set <- yardstick::metric_set(
  yardstick::accuracy, 
  yardstick::precision, 
  yardstick::recall, 
  yardstick::f_meas, 
  yardstick::spec
)
```


```{r}
preds <- read.csv("data/test_predictions.csv")
```

```{r}
preds <- preds %>% 
  mutate(FoodInsecure_flag = factor(FoodInsecure_flag, levels = c("Insecure","Secure")),pred_class = factor(.pred_class , levels = c("Insecure","Secure")))

rf_preds <- preds %>% filter(model=="Random forest")
lr_preds <- preds %>% filter(model=="Logistic regression")

nrow(rf_preds) ; nrow(lr_preds)
```
```{r}
#Producing a confusion matrix for each model 
conf_rf <- conf_mat(rf_preds , truth = FoodInsecure_flag , estimate = pred_class)
conf_rf


```
```{r}
lr_pred <- lr_preds %>% 
  mutate(.pred_class = factor(.pred_class , levels = c("Insecure" , "Secure")))
conf_lr <- conf_mat(lr_pred , truth=FoodInsecure_flag , estimate = .pred_class)
conf_lr
```
```{r}
metrics_set <- yardstick::metric_set(
  yardstick::accuracy, 
  yardstick::precision, 
  yardstick::recall, 
  yardstick::f_meas, 
  yardstick::spec
)

# Fix BOTH dataframes first, before any metrics are computed
rf_preds <- rf_preds %>%
  mutate(.pred_class = factor(.pred_class, levels = c("Insecure", "Secure")))
```


```{r}
lr_preds <- lr_preds %>%
  mutate(.pred_class = factor(.pred_class, levels = c("Insecure", "Secure")))
```


```{r}
# NOW compute metrics using the fixed data
rf_metrics <- rf_preds %>% metrics_set(truth = FoodInsecure_flag, estimate = .pred_class)
lr_metrics <- lr_preds %>% metrics_set(truth = FoodInsecure_flag, estimate = .pred_class)
```


```{r}
rf_auc <- rf_preds %>% yardstick::roc_auc(truth = FoodInsecure_flag, .pred_Insecure)
lr_auc <- lr_preds %>% yardstick::roc_auc(truth = FoodInsecure_flag, .pred_Insecure)
```


```{r}
rf_metrics; rf_auc
```


```{r}
lr_metrics; lr_auc
```

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
```


```{r }
roc_data <- preds %>% 
  group_by(model) %>% 
  roc_curve(truth = FoodInsecure_flag , .pred_Insecure)

ggplot(roc_data , aes(x= 1-specificity , y= sensitivity , color = model))+
  geom_path(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(lty = 3 ) +
  labs(title = "Roc Curve : Random Forest vs Logistic Regression") + 
  theme_minimal()

```
```{r}
rf_summary <- rf_metrics %>% 
  select(.metric , .estimate) %>% 
  mutate(model = "Random Forest")

lr_summary <- lr_metrics %>% 
  select(.metric , .estimate) %>%
  mutate(model = "Logistic Regression")

rf_auc_row <- tibble(.metric = "roc_auc", .estimate = rf_auc$.estimate , model = "Random Forest")

lr_auc_row <- tibble(.metric = "roc_auc", .estimate = lr_auc$.estimate , model = "Logistic Regression")

# Stacking everything together 
validation_matrix <- bind_rows(rf_summary , lr_summary , rf_auc_row , lr_auc_row) %>%
 pivot_wider(names_from = model , values_from = .estimate)

validation_matrix

```
```{r}
# Based on the validation matrix , Random Forest is selected as the final model. It outperforms Logistic Regression on ROC-AUC (0.840 vs 0.819), accuracy (0.840 vs 0.828) , precision (0.680 vs 0.569) and specificity (0.974 vs 0.953) meaning it ranks households mode reliably overall and produces far fewer alarms when it does flag a householf as food-insecure (68% of its positive flags are correct , vs 57% for Logistic Regression)

#Logistic Regression has slightly better recall and F1-score, but the difference is small. Random Forest performs better overall on most metrics, so it is the stronger model.

#However neither of the model performs well on recall at the default 0.5 cutoff both catch fewer than 3 in 10 actua; food insecure holdholds. This is the key limitation investigated in the next step.
```

```{r}

```

```{r}
rf_preds <- rf_preds %>%
  mutate(.pred_class_adj = if_else(.pred_Insecure > 0.3, "Insecure", "Secure")) %>%
  mutate(.pred_class_adj = factor(.pred_class_adj, levels = c("Insecure", "Secure")))

conf_mat(rf_preds , truth = FoodInsecure_flag , estimate = .pred_class_adj)
```


```{r}
yardstick::recall(rf_preds , truth = FoodInsecure_flag , estimate = .pred_class_adj)
```


```{r}
yardstick::precision(rf_preds , truth = FoodInsecure_flag , estimate = .pred_class_adj)
```
```{r}
#Lowering the classification threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 substantially improves recall , from 24.6% to 63.3% , the model now correctly identifies 481 to 760 food-insecure households , versus 187 at the default threshold. This comes at a real cost to precision , which drops from 68.0% to 48.8%: nearly half of households flagged as food-insecure at this threshold are false alarms 

# A 0.3 threshold catches more valuerabe households but also creates more false positives . it is better if missing a valuerable household is worse than incorrectly flagging one.
```

```{r}
# TASK 3 
rf_preds %>% 
  group_by(ProvinceCode) %>% 
  yardstick::recall(truth = FoodInsecure_flag, estimate = .pred_class)
```
```{r}
rf_preds %>% 
  filter(FoodInsecure_flag == "Insecure") %>% 
  count(ProvinceCode)
```
```{r}
# The recall rate is quite varied among the provinces , ranging from 5.0% in Province 9 to 35.1 in Province 5 almost seven times diffirence. Recall is not a matter of sample size alone because there are 20 genuine food insecure households in Province 9 test set of which only 1 has been recalled by the model. Similar is the case with province 7 where there is a low recall rate(13.0%) and a larger sample size(146 households).

# This creates a problem of fairnessm since a tool that is used for the purpose of prioritizing intervention efforts would, based on current configuration of the model , serve the food insecure households in Provinces 9 and 7 much less than those in Province 5 . Without additional exploration(wether is because of a smaller number of training cases in these two provinces , or due to diffireny predictor-food insecurity relationships , or some other reason) , this problem needs to be acknowleged 
```

```{r}
# By the technical sucess criteria set in Milestone 1 , the model performs well : ROC-AUC (0.840) comfortably exceeds the 0.75 threshold , more than the required 3 significant variables were identified , and both modelling approaches converge on the same key drivers (income , dwelling quality , province)

# However being able to meet the ROC-AUC threshold does not mean the model is ready to support the started business decision , Milestone 1's business objective is to help identify valuerable households for target intervention and at the model's default classification threshold intervention and at the model's default classification threshold , only 24.6% of genuinely food-insecure households are actually flagged. A high ROC-AUC reflects good ranking abilitu across all possible thresholds , but the specific threshold needed for practical deployment (catching enough at risk- households to inform real resource allocation ) was not part of the original technical success criteria , and is arguably a gap is in how sucess was originally defined.

#A threshold increase to 0.3 brings the recall up to 63.3% better matching the business goal, but it does come with the tradeoff of precision (48.8%), in that almost half of the identified cases would not actually experince food insecurity. This tradeoff and optimal threshold for the business goal need to be an intentional decision.
```

```{r}
# Association vs Causation
# The variable identified as important such as  income, dewelling quality , province , perceived income are associations that have been observed through the model analysis not as causative factors . For instance , individuals with low income face a high chance of being foof insecure ; however the findings does nit prove that increasing the income level alone can reduce food insecurity , as other factors not considered in the analysis (for instance , unexpected illness, food costs , job instability) may affect both the independent variable and the dependent variables. R6 risk from Milestone 1 predicted this same risj and concluded that findings should be considered associations and not causation. 
```
